title: Permutations of a String
excerpt: Take everything and decide the order. That small change moves the problem from 2 to the n up to n factorial, which puts a hard ceiling on what enumeration can ever solve.

content.text: Subsets asked which items to take. Permutations asks something different: take all of them, and decide what order to put them in. The change sounds small and it moves the problem into a much more expensive part of the world.
There are
n
choices for the first position,
for the second since one item is used up, and so on. That product is
n
factorial.

body.code:
n = 3    3 x 2 x 1 = 6 arrangements
n = 5    120
n = 10   3,628,800
n = 13   over 6 billion
n = 20   about 2.4 x 10^18, more than seconds since the universe began

content.text: Compare that against subsets. At 20 items subsets produces about a million answers, which a laptop handles without complaint. Permutations of 20 items produce more arrangements than there have been seconds since the beginning of the universe.

The practical consequence is worth stating plainly. If a problem asks you to enumerate permutations and the input can exceed roughly 10 or 11 items, enumeration is not the intended solution and you should be looking for a different approach entirely. Recognizing that boundary saves a lot of wasted effort.

body.text: The new difficulty: remembering what you used

content.text: Subsets kept order out of the way with a start index, and never needed to know which items were already taken, because it only ever looked forward.
Permutations cannot do that. Every remaining item is a legal next choice regardless of position, so the loop has to run over all of them, and you need some way to know which are still available.
The direct approach is a parallel array of booleans, one per item, marking whether it is currently placed. Before choosing item
i
you check the flag; if it is set, that item is somewhere above you in the current arrangement and cannot be used again.
The important detail is in the un-choose step. There are now
two

pieces of state to undo: the item comes off the arrangement and its flag goes back to false. Undo one and forget the other and the search goes wrong in a way that is genuinely difficult to read, because the arrangement looks correct while the availability flags no longer match it.
Step through and watch the used flags alongside the arrangement, since every time the recursion returns, both should change together.

body.text: The other way, which trades clarity for memory

content.text: There is a second standard approach, and it avoids the flags entirely.
Think of the array as split at position
k
: everything before it is decided, everything from
k
onward is still available. To choose an item for position
k
, swap it into place, recurse on
, then swap it back.

It uses no extra array and the un-choose is the same swap performed again, which is tidy. The cost is that the array gets scrambled during the search, so the items are not in their original order while you are inside the recursion. If a prune needs to know something about the original ordering, the used-array version is easier to reason about. Both produce the same set of permutations, occasionally in a different sequence.
Everything so far assumed the items are distinct. Give it
and it produces six answers where only three are actually different, because it treats the two 1s as separate objects.
The fix is a small piece of reasoning worth following, since the same pattern turns up in several problems.

Sort the input first so equal items sit next to each other. Then, among a run of identical items, allow only one fixed order of use: an item may be placed only if the identical item immediately before it has already been placed. That forces the copies to be used left to right, so each distinct arrangement is generated exactly once.
The condition reads oddly the first time. It says: if this item equals the previous one, and the previous one is
not
currently in use, then we are about to start a duplicate branch that a sibling has already handled, so skip it.

variants.code:
def permutations(items):
    answers, current = [], []
    used = [False] * len(items)

    def solve():
        if len(current) == len(items):
            answers.append(current[:])
            return

        for i in range(len(items)):
            if used[i]:
                continue              # already placed somewhere above

            used[i] = True            # choose
            current.append(items[i])
            solve()                   # explore
            current.pop()             # un-choose, both halves
            used[i] = False

    solve()
    return answers

content.text: Undoing only half the state.
The item is popped and the flag stays true, or the other way round. The symptom is answers that are too short or items that vanish from later branches.
Deduplicating without sorting first.
The skip rule relies on equal items being adjacent. Unsorted, it removes some duplicates and misses others, which is worse than doing nothing because the output looks nearly right.
Recording the arrangement without copying it.
The same bug as in subsets, and it bites harder here because the working array ends up back in its original order rather than empty, so every stored answer is the untouched input.
Trying to enumerate permutations of a large input.
If
n
can reach 15, no amount of pruning will save an enumeration. The problem wants something else.

questions.prompt: Why does the permutations loop start at 0 while the subsets loop starts at a passed-in index?

options.label: Any unused item may go next, so position no longer restricts the choice
Because permutations allow items to repeat
To make the answers come out in sorted order

questions.prompt: Your permutation solver returns arrangements shorter than the input. What is the likely cause?

options.label: The un-choose step restores only one of the two pieces of state
The base case compares against the wrong length
The used array was never initialized

questions.prompt: Roughly how many permutations does a 13-item list have?
Why must the input be sorted before applying the duplicate-skipping rule?

options.label: The rule compares each item with the one immediately before it, which only finds duplicates when equal items are adjacent
Because the answers must be produced in sorted order

seoTitle: Permutations of a String: Backtracking with Swap and Used Array
seoDescription: Permutations with backtracking: why n factorial rules out large inputs, tracking used items and undoing both halves of the state, the swap variant, and the sort-then-skip rule for duplicate elements.
